ig_caption:
Breslau, 20 July 1912. Stepan Levitsky had White against Frank Marshall in a French Defence at a big German tournament.

Marshall gave up a pawn so his knight could jump to d4, then took a bishop on h3 with his rook. When White's rook attacked his queen, he did not run. He put the queen on g3, where White could take it three ways. Each one loses: one ends in mate at once, one in mate on the back row, and the last leaves Black a piece up. Levitsky resigned on the spot.

Marshall later wrote that the spectators showered the board with gold coins. Other reports from the time say nothing of it, and some say the money was just bets being paid. Nobody knows for sure, so it is still called the Gold Coins Game.

Would you have seen 23...Qg3? 👇

slides.take: Stepan Levitsky, White, against Frank Marshall, Black, in a French Defence. Marshall lets White take the pawn on d5.
slides.edge: In return, his knight jumps to d4 and hits the queen on e2. Black's pieces are all pointing at White's king.

slides.title: A bishop taken
slides.moves: d4 e6 e4 d5 Nc3 c5 Nf3 Nc6 exd5 exd5 Be2 Nf6 O-O Be7 Bg5 O-O dxc5 Be6 Nd4 Bxc5 Nxe6 fxe6 Bg4 Qd6 Bh3 Rae8 Qd2 Bb4 Bxf6 Rxf6 Rad1 Qc5 Qe2 Bxc3 bxc3 Qxc3 Rxd5 Nd4 Qh5 Ref8 Re5 Rh6 Qg5 Rxh3 Rc5
slides.take: Black's rook takes the bishop on h3. White cannot take back: 23.gxh3 Nf3+ would fork king and queen.
slides.edge: So White hits back: 23.Rc5 attacks Black's queen on c3. Where should it go?

slides.title: The queen goes to g3
slides.moves: d4 e6 e4 d5 Nc3 c5 Nf3 Nc6 exd5 exd5 Be2 Nf6 O-O Be7 Bg5 O-O dxc5 Be6 Nd4 Bxc5 Nxe6 fxe6 Bg4 Qd6 Bh3 Rae8 Qd2 Bb4 Bxf6 Rxf6 Rad1 Qc5 Qe2 Bxc3 bxc3 Qxc3 Rxd5 Nd4 Qh5 Ref8 Re5 Rh6 Qg5 Rxh3 Rc5 Qg3
slides.take: 23...Qg3! The queen stands where the h-pawn, the f-pawn or White's queen can take it.
slides.edge: If White does nothing, 24...Qxh2 is mate. Levitsky looked, and resigned at once.

slides.title: If the h-pawn takes
slides.moves: d4 e6 e4 d5 Nc3 c5 Nf3 Nc6 exd5 exd5 Be2 Nf6 O-O Be7 Bg5 O-O dxc5 Be6 Nd4 Bxc5 Nxe6 fxe6 Bg4 Qd6 Bh3 Rae8 Qd2 Bb4 Bxf6 Rxf6 Rad1 Qc5 Qe2 Bxc3 bxc3 Qxc3 Rxd5 Nd4 Qh5 Ref8 Re5 Rh6 Qg5 Rxh3 Rc5 Qg3 hxg3 Ne2#
slides.take: 24.hxg3 Ne2 is mate. The knight checks from e2, and nothing can take it.
slides.edge: The rook on h3 covers h1 and h2. White's own pawns and rook fill the king's other squares.

slides.title: Every capture loses
slides.body: 24.fxg3 Ne2+ 25.Kh1 Rxf1 is mate on the back row. 24.Qxg3 Ne2+ 25.Kh1 Nxg3+ 26.Kg1 Nxf1 leaves Black a whole piece ahead.
slides.note: Not taking fails too: the threat of mate on h2 is still there.

slides.body: Marshall later wrote that the spectators showered the board with gold coins. Reports from the time do not mention it, and some say it was only bets being paid.
